'''Paul S. Anderson''' (born February 3, 1938) is an [[Americans|American]] [[chemist]].<ref name=OralHistory>{{cite book|last1=  Traynham |first1=James G.|title= Paul S. Anderson, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by James G. Traynham at Bristol-Myers Squibb Wilmington, Delaware on 28 October 2002|url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/anderson_ps_0266_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]]|date=October 28, 2002}}</ref> He worked at [[Merck & Co.|Merck]], DuPont-Merck, and [[Bristol-Myers Squibb]].

==Early life and education==
Paul S. Anderson was born February 3, 1938, in [[Concord, Vermont]], and grew up in [[Swanton (town), Vermont|Swanton, Vermont]].<ref name=UVF>{{cite web|title=Of Learning and Life|url=http://alumni.uvm.edu/foundation/celebrate/stories/anderson.php|website=The University of Vermont Foundation|accessdate=11 December 2014}}</ref> He attended Highgate High School, then went on to attend the [[University of Vermont]], receiving his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in chemistry in 1959. He then studied at the [[University of New Hampshire]], receiving his Ph.D. in chemistry in 1963. He briefly accepted a post-doctoral fellowship with [[Jerrold Meinwald]] at [[Cornell University]].<ref name=OralHistory/>

==Career==
Anderson accepted a senior research position at the Merck, Sharp & Dohme Research Laboratories.<ref name=OralHistory/>

==Awards==
In 1995 he received the E. B. Hershberg Award from the [[American Chemical Society]] for his work on medicinally-active substances.<ref name=Hershberg2>{{cite web|title=The E. B. Hershberg Award for Important Discoveries in Medicinally Active Substances|url=https://www.acsmedchem.org/?nd=hershbergaward|website=ACS Division of Medicinal Chemistry|accessdate=9 December 2014}}</ref><ref name=Hershberg>{{cite web|title=E. B. Hershberg Award for Important Discoveries in Medicinally Active Substances|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/e-b-hershberg-award-for-important-discoveries-in-medicinally-active-substances.html|website=American Chemical Society|accessdate=9 December 2014}}</ref> Other significant awards include the [[Perkin Medal]] in 2002, the [[NAS Award for Chemistry in Service to Society]] in 2003 and the [[Priestley Medal]] in 2006.<ref name=C&EN2005>{{cite journal|last1=Thayer|first1=Ann|title=Paul Anderson is Priestley Medalist|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=June 13, 2005|volume=83|issue=24|page=5|url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/news/83/i24/8324paulanderson.html|accessdate=9 December 2014|doi=10.1021/cen-v083n024.p005|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=ForbesProfile>{{cite web|title=Paul Anderson Profile|url=https://www.forbes.com/profile/paul-anderson/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141210000558/http://www.forbes.com/profile/paul-anderson/|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 10, 2014|work=Forbes|accessdate=9 December 2014}}</ref>

He was the 1997 President of the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name=ForbesProfile/><ref name=Anderson>{{cite web|title=Paul S. Anderson|url=https://medchem.ku.edu/sites/medchem.drupal.ku.edu/files/docs/awards/anderson.pdf|website=Department of Medicinal Chemistry|publisher=University of Kansas|accessdate=9 December 2014}}</ref>
